aliases: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
terms.definition: The American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a 1963 table that gives each of 128 characters (letters, digits, punctuation, and control signals) a number from 0 to 127.
terms.etymology: An acronym of American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

terms.definition: An agreed-upon table that turns characters into numbers, so that text can be stored and sent as bits.
The number a character encoding assigns to one character. In ASCII, the code point for A is 65.
An ASCII code (0 to 31, and 127) that prints nothing and instead tells a device to do something, such as start a new line or ring a bell.
A single binary digit, 0 or 1. Seven bits can make 2⁷ = 128 different patterns, which is exactly the size of ASCII.
terms.etymology: Short for binary digit, coined by John Tukey in the 1940s.

terms.definition: A font in which every character takes up the same width, so text lines up in a perfect grid. Terminals and ASCII games depend on this.
How bright a color looks to the human eye. Green counts the most and blue the least, so luminance ≈ 0.299·R + 0.587·G + 0.114·B.
A list of characters sorted from least ink to most ink, such as ' .:-=+*#%@'. ASCII art picks a character from the ramp for each pixel's brightness.
A screen and keyboard that shows only rows of text characters. Early computer users worked entirely through terminals.
A programming library written by Ken Arnold at UC Berkeley that lets a program place any character at any row and column of a terminal. Rogue was one of its first big users.
A game in the style of Rogue (1980): turn-based movement on a grid, a new randomly generated dungeon every play, and death that is permanent.
A rule where a character who dies is gone for good. You start a brand-new game, not from a save point.
Building game content, such as maps and cities, with an algorithm and random numbers instead of designing each piece by hand.
A game level stored as a grid of numbers or characters, where each value means a kind of square: floor, wall, door, and so on.
The worldwide character encoding with room for over a million characters, including every alphabet and emoji. Its first 128 code points are exactly ASCII.
